newsitem.title: USA: Bull market has right stuff; nothing in sight to trip it up.
newsitem.headline: Bull market has right stuff; nothing in sight to trip it up.

text.p: Can this bull market fly?
Stocks sprinted through new highs this week and the experts say there is nothing in the horizon that could trip up this incredible market.
The Dow Jones industrial average hurdled the 8,000-point barrier for the first time ever as good news about the economy and corporate earnings kept rolling in.
Indeed, the market has had a liking for breakthroughs and a distaste for standing still.

For the past two years, the Dow has soared 4,200 points, or nearly 110 percent. In the second quarter, the blue-chip market alone racked up a spectacular gain of 1,225 points after racing from a mid-April low at 6,392.
So far this year, the Dow is up nearly 25 percent, vs. a rise of 26 percent for all of 1996.
On Friday, profit taking pruned some of the Dow's gains to 7,890.46, off 130.31 points. For the week, it was off 31.36 points.
The jump in stocks has been fuelled by unexpectedly good corporate earnings, which have beat quarter on quarter the pessimistic views of many Wall Street experts.
The market has come to realise that what seemed at first to be outrageous expectations, actually turned out not to be outrageous after all.

The second-quarter earnings have been a mirror image of the past several quarters, fooling the Wall Street gurus who had thought that the stock market was an out of control beast that would fall on hard times this year.
The economy's growth has slowed enough to keep the Federal Reserve from flexing its interest-rate muscles and more importantly, inflation appears to be dead.
In the first six months of this year, consumer prices rose at their slowest pace in 11 years, and producer prices fell for a record sixth straight month in June.
There's more good news. At less than 5 percent, the unemployment rate is the lowest in nearly 25 years and consumer confidence is at a 28-year high.

"We're all breathing hard in this particularly thin atmosphere but there isn't anything on the horizon that suggests that the market will be presented with fundamental new information that will derail the bull market," said Russell Sheldon, senior economist at Mellon Economics.

"The Fed is likely on hold, inflation is good, the economy is growing moderately and earnings have been better than expected and there is no reason for that to change immediately," he said. "It's amazing but there's not much that would point to a major risk."
The analysts who have been predicting that the rise in earnings would end, have helped to create a market full of unexpected events.
Many market analysts had been chanting the same song for a long time that earnings would tumble. It became the opinion du jour and analysts who were the first to disagree, seemed in the wrong camp.
Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call, said the analysts have tended to low-ball their earnings forecasts after two years of blockbuster results.

"When things are this good and we've had such a sustained earnings recovery, the analysts start to get a little more conservative, and usually, they tend to shave the numbers down too much before the reporting period," he said.
Hill said the investment researchers lean to the low side on their estimates so as not to be blamed for causing major sell-offs in stocks due to earnings disappointments.
"This pattern repeats every quarter but Wall Street just doesn't really absorb this phenomena," he said.

"You get the normal negative bias in pre-earnings announcements by highly visible industries and people believe that the quarter is going to hell and they are all worried, then they get excited when the results turn out to be better than expected," Hill said.
James Dines, publisher of the Dines Letter in Belvedere, Calif., said the change in Corporate America's mind-set has also propelled the stock market.

"In the old days, management paid out half of its earnings in dividends, but now, instead of getting free tickets to the country club, the managers are given stock options in their companies and they're interested in pushing up their stock prices through stock buybacks," he said.
Dines did not rule out the possibility that the market could suffer a nasty spill.

"This is an emotional market," he said "There's a flood money coming into stock mutual funds through those automatic 401K plans and because stocks move on supply and demand instead of logic, we should all remember that bubbles are invisible to those inside the bubble and bubbles never pop slowly."
Dines said the "accidents" that could change things for the stock market include a sudden spike in inflation and problems in the currency or banking systems.
But for now, Dines sees no end to the bull run, and forecasts that the Dow could reach the 10,000 level by the end of this year.
"It's only 2,000 points away from there and at the rate we're going, we might be even higher," Dines said.
On Friday, the Nasdaq composite index lost 20.86 points to close at 1,547.99, but was up 45.37 points for the week.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks was off 16.31 to 915.30 and lost 1.38 for the week. The American Stock Exchange index was off 3.75 to 633.59, and down 1.88 for the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks was off 6.99 to 475.97, and lost 2.15 for the week.
